en.title: Education Biology: the whole course
en.short: What Education Biology covers, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Education Biology joins the study of living things to the study of how people learn and how to teach biology well. It prepares teachers for secondary schools, colleges and related settings. The degree has two halves. One half is biology: cells, organisms, genetics, ecology, physiology, microbiology, evolution and biotechnology. The other is education: learning, curriculum, methods, assessment, laboratory work and teaching practice. The halves must speak to each other. A teacher who knows biology but cannot explain it, manage a class or assess fairly is incomplete. A teacher who knows methods but not the subject cannot answer a curious student’s question. The course trains subject knowledge and professional judgement.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text: Awards and lengths differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, universities commonly offer B.Ed. or B.Sc.(Ed.) Biology as four-year full-time bachelor’s programmes, while colleges of education offer the Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE), commonly over three years. The National Universities Commission (NUC) regulates university programmes and the National Commission for Colleges of Education (NCCE) regulates NCE programmes. In Ghana, colleges of education and universities offer teacher education, and in the United Kingdom routes include a B.Ed. or a subject degree followed by a Postgraduate Certificate in Education (PGCE). Titles and routes vary. Check your own handbook for current length, award, accreditation and teaching-practice rules. Programmes usually combine lectures, practicals, micro-teaching, school observation and block teaching practice. Some include a final-year project.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage starts with the nature and scope of biology education and an introduction to education and teaching. You then meet educational psychology for biology teachers, the chemistry and physics needed for biology, and the mathematics and statistics used in practicals and research. Laboratory safety and biological techniques come early because they govern every later practical. The first biology blocks cover cell biology, plant and animal diversity, genetics foundations, and ecology and environment.

The core stage deepens subject and profession together. You study plant and animal anatomy and physiology, microbiology and immunology, molecular biology and biotechnology, evolution and systematics, and population and applied genetics. In parallel you study the biology curriculum and syllabus, methods of teaching biology, instructional materials and ICT, assessment and evaluation, laboratory management and fieldwork, inclusive and differentiated teaching, and environmental and health education. Teaching practice puts these ideas under real classroom conditions. Research methods and ethics prepare you to inquire into your own teaching and act responsibly.

Master’s work is more advanced and research-led. It includes advanced learning theories, research methods and dissertation work, curriculum leadership and policy, and frontiers in biology and bioinformatics.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study the two halves together. When you learn a biological concept, prepare a short explanation for a named class level, with one example and one question. When you learn a teaching method, apply it to a biology topic.

For biology, draw and label diagrams from memory, then check them. Do calculations step by step and keep units. For practicals, read the protocol before class, write your own risk notes, and record results as you go. For education, use classroom observation. Note what the teacher did, what students did, and what evidence showed learning.

Use your national syllabus and your institution’s handbook as working documents. Syllabi and regulations change, so check the current official version. Form a study group that explains topics aloud; teaching a topic is the best test of understanding.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Many students treat education courses as secondary and revise biology only. That is a mistake, because teaching practice and professional courses shape how you explain the subject. Others memorise definitions without using them. In genetics, they learn terms but cannot solve a cross. In ecology, they confuse a food chain with a food web, or correlation with cause.

In practical work, common faults are ignoring safety rules, tasting unknown substances, and leaving Bunsen burners or cultures unattended. In teaching, students prepare content without checking the syllabus level, talk for the whole lesson, or use ICT as decoration rather than a learning tool. In research, some copy sources without citation or claim more than their sample can support. Another mistake is assuming that one country’s curriculum, examinations or laboratory rules apply everywhere. Name the country and check the current official source.

keyPoints: Education Biology combines biology subject knowledge with the professional study of teaching.
Awards, programme lengths and teaching-practice rules differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
The introductory stage builds subject foundations and first teaching ideas; the core stage deepens both.
Study biology and education together by turning each concept into a short lesson explanation.
Practical safety and accurate measurement are part of the subject, not extras.
Name the country when you state a curriculum, examination or laboratory rule, and check the current official source.

en.title: Nature and Scope of Biology Education
en.short: The meaning, aims, curriculum place and teacher roles of biology education, and how biology and education connect.

sections.heading: Meaning and aims
sections.text: Biology education is the study of how people learn biology and how it is taught. It joins biological knowledge with educational theory and practice. Its aims include scientific literacy, which means understanding basic biological ideas and using evidence; practical and thinking skills; healthy living and care for the environment; positive attitudes to science; and preparation for further study and work. In a teacher-education degree such as B.Sc.(Ed) or B.Ed in Nigeria, students study both biology and education.

sections.heading: In the school curriculum
sections.text: School science curricula usually introduce biology within general science at lower secondary level, then as a separate subject at upper secondary level. This pattern varies by country, so check the current national curriculum. Biology is included because it helps learners understand life, health and the environment, and because it supports careers in medicine, agriculture, teaching and research. The curriculum states aims, content and expected practical work; the teacher turns these into lessons.

sections.heading: Science and education
sections.text: Biology as a science builds explanations from observation, experiment and evidence. Education as a professional field studies learning, teaching, assessment and the ethics of working with young people. A biology teacher needs both. Pedagogical content knowledge, often shortened to PCK, is the special mix of subject knowledge and teaching knowledge that lets a teacher explain an idea, choose a useful example and spot common misunderstandings. For example, Mr Adeyemi, an invented teacher in Ibadan, plans a lesson on local crop pests by checking the syllabus, choosing a safe activity and assessing what learners understand.

sections.heading: Roles of the teacher
sections.text: A biology teacher is a planner, who prepares lessons from the syllabus; a facilitator, who guides learners through questions and practical work; and an assessor, who checks learning fairly. The teacher also manages the laboratory safely, keeps records, mentors learners, communicates with parents or guardians, and acts as a role model. Because biology and education both change, the teacher must keep reading, reflect on lessons and attend continuing professional development.

keyPoints: Biology education joins biological knowledge with educational theory and practice.
Its aims include scientific literacy, practical skills, health and environmental awareness, and preparation for further study and work.
Biology usually appears in general science at lower secondary and as a separate subject at upper secondary, but this varies by country.
Check the current national curriculum for aims, content and practical work.
Pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) is the mix of subject knowledge and teaching knowledge that helps a teacher explain ideas and anticipate misunderstandings.
A biology teacher plans, facilitates, assesses, manages safety and records, mentors learners and keeps learning professionally.

en.title: Introduction to Education and Teaching
en.short: This summary covers education, schooling, teaching roles, school systems, lesson observation and reflection.

sections.heading: Education and schooling
sections.text: Education is the lifelong process of gaining knowledge, skills, values and understanding. Schooling is the formal, organised instruction given in schools. Teaching is the planned guidance of learning, and pedagogy is the study of how teaching is done. The three are linked but not the same: much education happens outside school, and schooling is only one way of providing it. A curriculum is the planned content and learning experiences of a course or school.

sections.heading: Teacher roles
sections.text: A teacher plans lessons, explains ideas, asks questions, sets tasks, assesses learning and manages the classroom. Teachers also guide learners, keep records, report progress and work with parents and colleagues. The balance changes with the age of learners, the subject and the country. In biology teaching, the teacher also organises practical work and fieldwork safely, but those skills are covered later in this course.

sections.heading: School systems
sections.text: A school system is the organised network of schools, rules, funding and examinations in a country or region. It usually has levels such as early childhood, primary, secondary and tertiary education, and may include public, private and religious schools. Systems differ by country. In Nigeria, for example, schools are commonly grouped into basic, senior secondary and tertiary levels, but the exact years, examinations and rules are set by national policy and can change, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Observation and reflection
sections.text: Lesson observation means watching a lesson with a clear focus and recording what teachers and learners do. It is not just judging the teacher; it is collecting evidence to understand learning. Reflective practice means thinking carefully about an experience, asking what happened, why it happened and what to change next time. A simple cycle is plan, teach, observe, reflect, then act. For example, Amina, a first-year student teacher, observes a biology lesson and notes how questions were asked and how time was used. Afterwards she writes what she saw, why it may have worked, and one change she will try.

keyPoints: Education is lifelong learning; schooling is formal instruction; teaching guides learning.
Teachers plan, instruct, assess, manage and guide, and their roles vary by level and country.
School systems have levels, rules and examinations, and they differ by country.
Lesson observation collects evidence about teaching and learning, not just judgement.
Reflective practice uses what happened to plan a change.
A useful cycle is plan, teach, observe, reflect, act.

en.title: Educational Psychology for Biology Teachers
en.short: Covers learning theories, motivation, adolescent development, memory and individual differences in biology classrooms.

sections.heading: Learning theories
sections.text: Behaviourism treats learning as a change in behaviour produced by reinforcement, such as praise or corrective feedback. It helps establish routines and clear expectations, but it explains understanding poorly. Constructivism says learners build new ideas on what they already know, so a biology teacher must first reveal misconceptions, for example the common belief that plants take food from soil. Cognitivism studies mental processes and notes that working memory is limited. Social learning theory adds that learners imitate models. In planning, begin with prior knowledge, use concrete examples, and model scientific language. In questioning, ask why and how, and allow wait time.

sections.heading: Motivation and adolescence
sections.text: Motivation is the drive to begin and sustain learning. Intrinsic motivation comes from interest or satisfaction; extrinsic motivation comes from rewards or pressure. Adolescents usually grow in abstract reasoning, so they can handle genetics and evolution, but development varies. Identity formation also matters, so respect and privacy are important in lessons on reproduction and health. A case: Mr Ade introduces genetics with family resemblance, lets learners predict, then gives a choice of a poster or a short report. Relevance, success and some choice support motivation without lowering standards.

sections.heading: Memory and differences
sections.text: Working memory holds only a few items at once, while long-term memory stores organised knowledge called schemas. Cognitive load theory warns against splitting attention, so a diagram should be explained beside it, not with a separate long text. Retrieval practice, such as low-stakes quizzes, and spaced practice, revisiting topics after days, strengthen memory more than rereading. Individual differences include prior knowledge, language, disability and pace. Learning styles, the idea that each student learns best through one sense, lack strong evidence; vary methods for the content, not to match labels. Support includes glossaries, bilingual word lists, scaffolds and flexible grouping.

keyPoints: Behaviourism uses reinforcement, while constructivism builds on prior knowledge and misconceptions.
Working memory is limited, so avoid cognitive overload and split attention.
Retrieval practice and spaced practice strengthen long-term memory.
Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation affect effort; relevance and choice help.
Adolescent abstract reasoning and identity develop at different rates, so privacy and respect matter.
Learning styles lack strong evidence; support prior knowledge, language and disability instead.

en.title: Chemistry and Physics for Biology
en.short: Water, pH, biomolecules, diffusion, osmosis, energy, light, temperature and basic instruments in living systems.

sections.heading: Water and pH
sections.text:
Water is polar: its oxygen atom pulls electrons, leaving partial charges. This allows hydrogen bonds, so water dissolves salts and sugars, carries heat, and has high specific heat capacity, the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 °C. Living systems use water as solvent and temperature buffer.

pH = −log10[H+] measures hydrogen ion concentration. A solution with [H+] = 1 × 10^-7 mol/L has pH 7, neutral at 25 °C. Enzymes work within narrow pH ranges, so a change can slow reactions.

sections.heading: Biomolecules
sections.text:
Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids are the main biomolecules, the molecules of life, built mainly from carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus. Small units called monomers join by condensation, which releases water; hydrolysis splits polymers using water.

Protein shape depends on amino acid sequence and determines function. Lipids store energy and form membranes. Nucleic acids store genetic information.

sections.heading: Movement and energy
sections.text:
Diffusion is net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration. Osmosis is diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, one that lets some substances pass, from higher water potential to lower water potential. Water potential is lower when more solute is dissolved.

ATP, adenosine triphosphate, is the cell’s energy currency. Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate releases energy. Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy in glucose; respiration releases it for cell work.

sections.heading: Light, heat, instruments
sections.text:
Light intensity affects photosynthesis rate until another factor, such as carbon dioxide or temperature, limits it. Temperature affects enzyme-catalysed reactions. Most human enzymes work best near 37 °C; high heat denatures them, so shape and activity are lost.

Instruments extend observation. Magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens. A 10× eyepiece with a 40× objective gives 10 × 40 = 400×. Thermometers, pH meters and spectrophotometers measure temperature, acidity and light absorption.

keyPoints: Water is polar, forms hydrogen bonds, and acts as a solvent and temperature buffer.
pH = −log10[H+], so [H+] = 1 × 10^-7 mol/L gives pH 7 at 25 °C.
Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids are the main biomolecules; condensation joins monomers and hydrolysis splits polymers.
Diffusion moves particles down a concentration gradient, while osmosis moves water across a selectively permeable membrane from higher to lower water potential.
ATP is the cell’s energy currency, and photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy.
Enzyme activity has an optimum temperature, and magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens, so 10× and 40× give 400×.

en.title: Mathematics and Statistics for Biology
en.short: Units, ratios, percentages, magnification, graphs, averages, variation, probability and sampling.

sections.heading: Units and proportions
sections.text: Biology uses common metric units: metre (m), kilogram (kg), litre (L) and mole (mol). Convert within a unit before calculating: 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 mm = 1,000 µm, 1 µm = 1,000 nm. A ratio compares two quantities, such as 3 red flowers to 1 white flower (3:1). A percentage is a part per hundred: percentage = (part ÷ whole) × 100. If 18 of 60 seeds germinate, germination is 18 ÷ 60 × 100 = 30%. Keep units with every answer.

sections.heading: Magnification and graphs
sections.text: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Use the same units. If a drawing of a 0.5 mm cell is 30 mm long, magnification = 30 ÷ 0.5 = 60×. Rearrange to find actual size: actual = image ÷ magnification. Choose graphs to suit data: bar charts for categories, line graphs for continuous change, scatter graphs for relationships. Label axes with quantity and unit, and give a clear title.

sections.heading: Averages and variation
sections.text: The mean is the sum divided by the number of values: mean = Σx ÷ n. The median is the middle value when ordered; the mode is the most frequent. The range = highest − lowest. The mean uses all values but is pulled by outliers (unusually high or low values); the median resists them. Variation is spread. Standard deviation measures how far values lie from the mean, but the range is quicker. For class scores 40, 50, 60, 70, 80: mean = 300 ÷ 5 = 60; median = 60; range = 40.

sections.heading: Probability and sampling
sections.text: Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. If 7 of 10 seeds germinate, P(germinate) = 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7 or 70%. A population is all individuals of interest; a sample is a part used to estimate it. Random sampling gives every individual an equal chance and reduces bias. Systematic sampling takes every nth item; stratified sampling samples within groups. Small or biased samples give unreliable summaries. Report sample size and method.

keyPoints: Convert to the same unit before calculating; 1 cm = 10 mm and 1 mm = 1,000 µm.
Percentage = (part ÷ whole) × 100, and magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; median is the middle value; mode is the most frequent; range = highest − lowest.
The mean is affected by outliers, so compare it with the median and report variation.
Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, and lies between 0 and 1.
Random sampling reduces bias; report the sample size and method with any summary.

en.title: Laboratory Safety and Biological Techniques
en.short: Personal safety, hazard symbols, chemicals and specimens, first aid, microscopy, staining, dissection and disposal.

sections.heading: Safety first
sections.text: Personal safety starts before practical work. Wear goggles, a lab coat and closed shoes, tie back long hair, and remove loose jewellery. Never eat, drink or taste in the laboratory. Know where the fire extinguisher, first-aid box, eyewash and exit are, and never work alone. Hazard symbols, often the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) pictograms, warn of flammable, corrosive, toxic or irritant substances. Learn the symbols on every bottle. Rules differ by country and school, so follow local policy.

sections.heading: Chemicals and specimens
sections.text: Handle chemicals only as instructed. Read the label, use the smallest amount, keep bottles closed, and never smell or taste a chemical directly. Use gloves and a fume cupboard when the label or teacher says so. Treat specimens as possible sources of infection: wear gloves and wash hands afterwards. Case: in a school in Accra, a learner finds an unlabelled bottle. The safe action is to tell the teacher, not to open it.

sections.heading: Microscope and staining
sections.text: Carry a microscope with two hands, one under the base and one on the arm. Place it away from the bench edge. Start with the low-power objective, use the coarse focus only on low power, then fine focus. Clean lenses with lens tissue, not clothing. Simple staining makes cells easier to see: place a drop of stain such as methylene blue on the specimen, add a cover slip, and avoid air bubbles. Use stain sparingly and wash it off your skin.

sections.heading: Dissection and disposal
sections.text: For dissection, follow instructions, keep sharp tools pointed away from your body, cut on a tray, and wash hands afterwards. Record work in pencil: draw clear lines, label parts, and note the magnification, date and specimen. Dispose of waste correctly: sharps in a sharps container, glass in a glass bin, chemical and biological waste as local rules require. For first aid, rinse a chemical splash with plenty of water and tell the teacher at once. Do not neutralise a spill unless trained. Know who the first-aider is.

keyPoints: Wear goggles, a lab coat and closed shoes, and know the hazard symbols before starting practical work.
Read chemical labels, use the smallest amount, and never taste or smell chemicals directly.
Carry a microscope with two hands and use the coarse focus only on low power.
Simple stains such as methylene blue make cells visible; use them sparingly.
During dissection, keep sharp tools away from your body and wash hands afterwards.
Dispose of sharps, glass and biological waste by local rules, and rinse chemical splashes with plenty of water before telling the teacher.

en.title: Cell Biology: Structure, Transport, Energy and Division
en.short: Cell structure, membranes, enzymes, respiration, photosynthesis, mitosis and cell diversity.

sections.heading: Cell structure and diversity
sections.text: Cells are the smallest living units. Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, have neither. Main organelles: nucleus holds DNA; mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration; ribosomes make proteins; endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus make and package materials; lysosomes digest. Plant cells usually have a cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole. Animal cells lack walls and chloroplasts and have small vacuoles. Microbial cells vary: bacteria are prokaryotic; fungi are eukaryotic with chitin walls; protozoa are eukaryotic without walls. Viruses are not cells.

sections.heading: Membranes and enzymes
sections.text: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins. It is selectively permeable. Diffusion moves small molecules from high to low concentration. Osmosis is water diffusion across a membrane. Facilitated diffusion uses proteins and no energy. Active transport uses ATP energy to move substances against a gradient. Endocytosis and exocytosis move larger materials in vesicles. Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy. Each has an active site and is specific to its substrate. High temperature or extreme pH denatures enzymes, changing shape and stopping activity.

sections.heading: Energy release and capture
sections.text: Respiration releases energy from glucose. Aerobic respiration starts with glycolysis in the cytoplasm and continues in mitochondria: glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + ATP energy. Anaerobic respiration gives less energy and produces lactate in animals or ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast. Photosynthesis captures light energy in chloroplasts: carbon dioxide + water gives glucose + oxygen, using light and chlorophyll. It has light-dependent and light-independent stages. The two processes are complementary.

sections.heading: Cell cycle and mitosis
sections.text: The cell cycle is the sequence from one division to the next. Interphase includes G1, S and G2; DNA replicates in S phase. Mitosis has prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, then cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm. Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells for growth and repair. Example: a cell with 8 chromosomes replicates its DNA, then each daughter cell receives 8 chromosomes, not 16.

keyPoints: Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells do not.
Plant cells usually have a cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole; animal cells do not.
The cell membrane is selectively permeable; diffusion and osmosis are passive, while active transport uses ATP.
Enzymes are specific protein catalysts; high heat or extreme pH denatures them.
Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + ATP energy; photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water gives glucose + oxygen using light.
Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells after DNA replication in S phase.

en.title: Plant and Animal Diversity
en.short: Classification, binomial names, major plant, animal and microorganism groups, adaptations and life cycles.

sections.heading: Classifying life
sections.text:
Classification arranges organisms by shared features. Taxonomy names and groups them; systematics studies evolutionary relationships. Main ranks are domain, kingdom, phylum (division in plants), class, order, family, genus and species. A dichotomous key identifies specimens by paired choices. Groups and names can change as evidence grows.

Begin with observable features, then use cell type, body plan and reproduction. Pupils can group local leaves, insects and fungi, then compare with accepted classification.

sections.heading: Binomial names
sections.text:
Binomial nomenclature gives each species a two-part Latin name: the genus with a capital letter, and the specific epithet in lower case. Write it in italics, or underline it by hand. Examples are Zea mays for maize and Musca domestica for the housefly.

Names follow international codes: the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi and plants, and the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature for animals. Common names vary, so scientific names aid clear communication. Use local names alongside them.

sections.heading: Major groups
sections.text:
Plants include bryophytes (mosses and liverworts, no vascular tissue), pteridophytes (ferns, vascular tissue and spores), gymnosperms (seeds not enclosed in fruit) and angiosperms (flowering plants, seeds in fruit). Animals include invertebrates, which lack a backbone, such as arthropods, molluscs and annelids, and vertebrates: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

Microorganisms include bacteria and archaea (prokaryotes), fungi such as yeasts and moulds, protozoa, algae, and viruses. Viruses are acellular and not usually classed as living cells. These groups are broad.

sections.heading: Adaptations and cycles
sections.text:
Adaptations are inherited features that aid survival. Xerophytes reduce water loss; hydrophytes have air spaces; animals show camouflage, gills or limbs suited to habitat. In life cycles, plants alternate haploid gametophyte and diploid sporophyte generations; insects and frogs show metamorphosis; bacteria divide by binary fission; yeasts bud.

In a school compound, compare cassava (Manihot esculenta), a goat and a mushroom, then classify them with a key. Collect ethically and return live specimens.

keyPoints: Classification groups organisms by shared features in a hierarchy from domain to species.
Binomial nomenclature uses a genus and specific epithet, written in italics, under international codes.
Major plant groups are bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.
Major animal groups include invertebrates and vertebrates; microorganisms include bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses.
Adaptations are inherited features that improve survival in a habitat.
Life cycles include alternation of generations in plants, metamorphosis in some animals, and binary fission or budding in microorganisms.

en.title: Genetics Foundations: Inheritance and Variation
en.short: This summary covers Mendelian crosses, probability, chromosomes, sex determination, variation, test crosses and pedigrees.

sections.heading: Mendel and monohybrid
sections.text: Mendel’s law of segregation says the two alleles of a gene separate when gametes form, so each gamete carries one. His law of independent assortment says alleles of different genes assort independently when they are on different chromosomes or far apart on the same chromosome. An allele is a version of a gene; genotype is the allele pair; phenotype is the visible trait. A monohybrid cross of true-breeding tall (TT) and short (tt) peas gives all Tt tall F1. Selfing F1 gives genotype ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt and phenotype ratio 3 tall : 1 short under complete dominance.

sections.heading: Dihybrid and probability
sections.text: A dihybrid cross follows two genes, such as seed shape (R round, r wrinkled) and colour (Y yellow, y green). RrYy × RrYy gives 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green if the genes assort independently. Probability uses the product rule for independent events: round yellow = 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16. The sum rule adds mutually exclusive outcomes. Check: 9/16 + 3/16 + 3/16 + 1/16 = 1.

sections.heading: Chromosomes, sex, variation
sections.text: Chromosomes are DNA and protein structures. Most human body cells are diploid (2n = 46), with 23 pairs; gametes are haploid (n = 23). In humans, females are XX and males XY, so the father’s sperm determines sex: X sperm gives XX, Y sperm gives XY. Variation is difference among individuals. It comes from mutation, recombination in meiosis, random fertilisation, and environment. Continuous variation, such as height, shows a range; discontinuous variation has distinct classes. A test cross identifies an unknown genotype by crossing it with a homozygous recessive. If a tall pea of unknown genotype crossed with tt gives any short offspring, the parent was Tt; if all are tall, it was TT. In a pedigree, squares are male, circles female, shaded means affected. A recessive pedigree often skips generations; a dominant one tends to appear in every generation.

keyPoints: Mendel’s law of segregation says alleles separate in gamete formation, and independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes or far apart on the same chromosome.
A monohybrid cross Tt × Tt gives genotype ratio 1:2:1 and phenotype ratio 3:1 under complete dominance.
A dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy gives 9:3:3:1 if the genes assort independently.
For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B); for mutually exclusive events, add the probabilities.
Human body cells are diploid (2n = 46) and gametes haploid (n = 23); the father’s sperm determines sex: XX female, XY male.
A test cross uses a homozygous recessive, and pedigrees show inheritance patterns though small families can mislead.

en.title: Ecology and Environment
en.short: Ecosystems, populations, energy flow, nutrient cycles, human impact and conservation.

sections.heading: Ecosystems and communities
sections.text: An ecosystem is a community of living things together with the non-living parts of their environment, such as soil, water, air and sunlight. A community is all the populations living in one area. A population is a group of one species in that area. These levels connect: a change in one population can affect the whole community. Ecologists study both small systems, such as a pond, and large ones, such as a forest.

sections.heading: Populations and interactions
sections.text: Population size changes through births, deaths, immigration and emigration. Resources such as food, water and space limit growth. Species interact in several ways: competition for resources, predation, mutualism (both benefit), and parasitism (one benefits, one is harmed). These interactions shape community structure. A simple case: if a school stream near Ibadan receives refuse, sensitive insects may disappear, and fish that eat them decline. Removing refuse and planting riverbank trees can help the stream recover.

sections.heading: Energy flow and cycles
sections.text: Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight. Producers, mainly plants, convert it by photosynthesis into chemical energy. Consumers eat producers or other consumers, and decomposers break down dead matter. Energy is lost as heat at each step, so food chains are short. A rough teaching guide is that about 10% passes to the next level, but real values vary. If producers hold 20,000 kJ, at 10% primary consumers get 2,000 kJ, secondary consumers 200 kJ, and tertiary consumers 20 kJ. Nutrients such as carbon and nitrogen cycle, not flow one way; decomposers return them to the soil.

sections.heading: Human impact and conservation
sections.text: Human activities can damage ecosystems through habitat loss, pollution, overexploitation and climate change. Conservation aims to protect biodiversity and ecosystem services, such as clean water and fertile soil. It includes protected areas, sustainable use, restoration and environmental education. Local action matters: a school can survey a nearby stream, record organisms, and report pollution. As a biology teacher, use such examples to connect ecology to learners’ lives. Check current national environmental laws and local rules before organising fieldwork.

keyPoints: An ecosystem is the community plus its non-living environment; a population is one species, and a community is all populations in an area.
Energy flows one way and is lost as heat; only a small fraction, often about 10%, passes to the next trophic level, and this varies.
If producers hold 20,000 kJ, at 10% transfer primary consumers get 2,000 kJ, secondary 200 kJ and tertiary 20 kJ.
Nutrients such as carbon and nitrogen are recycled by decomposers.
Species interactions include competition, predation, mutualism and parasitism.
Human impact includes habitat loss, pollution, overexploitation and climate change; conservation combines protection, sustainable use, restoration and education.

en.title: Plant Anatomy and Physiology
en.short: Plant tissues, transport, transpiration, photosynthesis, respiration, growth and hormones.

sections.heading: Tissues and organs
sections.text: Plants have meristematic tissue, which divides, and permanent tissue, which does not. Simple permanent tissues are parenchyma (packing, storage), collenchyma (flexible support) and sclerenchyma (rigid support). Xylem and phloem are complex tissues. Xylem carries water and minerals upward in dead vessels and tracheids. Phloem carries sugars both ways in living sieve tubes with companion cells. Root, stem and leaf are the main vegetative organs.

sections.heading: Water and transpiration
sections.text:
Water enters root hairs by osmosis and rises in xylem as a continuous column. Transpiration is water vapour loss, mainly through stomata. Cohesion and tension pull the column up; root pressure gives a small push. Light, warmth, wind and dry air raise transpiration; humidity lowers it. Guard cells open and close stomata. A potometer measures water uptake, which is used to estimate the transpiration rate.

Example: 12 cm3 in 30 minutes gives 12 ÷ 30 = 0.4 cm3 per minute. Over 20 cm2 of leaf, that is 0.4 ÷ 20 = 0.02 cm3 per cm2 per minute.

sections.heading: Photosynthesis and respiration
sections.text: Photosynthesis uses light, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Light reactions occur in thylakoids; the Calvin cycle fixes carbon in the stroma. Respiration releases energy from glucose: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + ATP. Glycolysis occurs in cytoplasm; the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain occur in mitochondria. Photosynthesis stores energy; respiration releases it.

sections.heading: Growth and adaptations
sections.text: Growth occurs at meristems: apical meristems lengthen roots and shoots; lateral cambium thickens stems. Hormones coordinate growth: auxin controls elongation and tropisms, gibberellin promotes elongation and germination, cytokinin promotes cell division, abscisic acid closes stomata and promotes dormancy, and ethylene ripens fruit. Xerophytes have thick cuticles and sunken stomata; hydrophytes have air spaces. Simple experiments include the starch test on a destarched variegated leaf, limewater with germinating seeds, and a potometer.

keyPoints: Meristematic tissue divides; permanent tissues include parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem.
Xylem carries water and minerals upward; phloem carries sugars both ways.
Transpiration is water vapour loss through stomata, driven by cohesion and tension.
Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2; respiration: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + ATP.
Auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid and ethylene control growth and responses.
Transpiration rate = water lost ÷ time; divide by leaf area for rate per unit area.

en.title: Animal Anatomy and Physiology
en.short: Animal tissues, organ systems, vertebrate comparisons and homeostasis for biology teachers.

sections.heading: Tissues and systems
sections.text: Animal anatomy is structure; physiology is function. Four basic tissues: epithelial (covering and lining, exchange), connective (support, blood, bone, fat), muscle (contraction: skeletal, cardiac, smooth), nervous (neurones conduct impulses). Tissues form organs and organ systems. In vertebrates, systems work together: circulation, respiration, digestion, excretion, nervous and endocrine control. A fish, frog, bird and mammal table helps teaching.

sections.heading: Circulation and respiration
sections.text: Circulation moves gases, nutrients, wastes and heat. Fish have a single circuit and a two-chambered heart (one atrium, one ventricle). Amphibians have two atria and one ventricle; most reptiles have three chambers, crocodilians four; birds and mammals have four chambers and two circuits. Respiration: gills in fish, skin and lungs in amphibians, lungs in reptiles, birds and mammals. Birds have air sacs and unidirectional airflow. Mammalian lungs use alveoli; gills use lamellae. Both give thin, moist, large exchange surfaces. Surface area to volume ratio falls with size: a cube of side 1 cm has surface area 6 cm² and volume 1 cm³, ratio 6 per cm; side 2 cm gives 24 cm² and 8 cm³, ratio 3 per cm. So large animals need specialised systems.

sections.heading: Digestion and excretion
sections.text: Digestion breaks food into absorbable molecules. Monogastric mammals have a stomach and small intestine; ruminants have a four-chambered stomach with microbes. Birds have a crop, proventriculus (glandular stomach), gizzard and caeca. Villi and microvilli increase absorptive area. Excretion removes nitrogenous waste. Aquatic fish excrete mostly ammonia, mammals urea, birds and many reptiles uric acid, which saves water. Kidneys filter blood; nephrons reabsorb useful substances. Compare freshwater and marine fish: freshwater fish gain water and lose salts, marine bony fish lose water and gain salts.

sections.heading: Control and homeostasis
sections.text: Nervous control is fast and electrical; endocrine control is slower and chemical. Neurones carry impulses; hormones travel in blood and act on target cells. Negative feedback keeps internal conditions near a set point. Examples: body temperature, blood glucose, water balance. Endotherms (birds, mammals) generate heat; ectotherms rely on environment. In teaching, use diagrams, models and comparative tables; if dissection is used, follow local safety and ethics rules.

keyPoints: The four basic animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.
Fish have a single circuit and a two-chambered heart; birds and mammals have four chambers and two circuits.
Gills, lungs and skin are exchange surfaces with thin, moist, large areas.
Nitrogenous waste is excreted mainly as ammonia in aquatic fish, urea in mammals and uric acid in birds and many reptiles.
Negative feedback keeps temperature, glucose and water balance near a set point.
Surface area to volume ratio = surface area ÷ volume; it falls as body size increases.

en.title: Microbiology and Immunology for Biology Teachers
en.short: Microorganisms, growth and control, immunity, vaccines and common infectious diseases.

sections.heading: Microorganisms
sections.text: Microorganisms are living things too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria are prokaryotes: single cells without a nucleus. Fungi are eukaryotes; yeasts are single-celled and moulds form hyphae. Viruses are not cells. They are obligate intracellular parasites, meaning they reproduce only inside a host cell. Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes, and some cause disease. Algae are mainly photosynthetic. Many microbes are harmless or useful; only some are pathogens, organisms that cause disease.

sections.heading: Growth and control
sections.text: Bacteria usually multiply by binary fission. In a closed culture the population shows lag, log, stationary and death phases. Culture needs nutrients, moisture, temperature and pH; agar plates and aseptic technique are common. Sterilization kills all microbes, including spores. Disinfection reduces pathogens on surfaces, and antiseptics are used on skin. Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, and misuse drives antimicrobial resistance. Worked example: if a bacterium divides every 20 minutes, 2 hours is 120 ÷ 20 = 6 generations. Starting with 100 cells: 100 × 2⁶ = 100 × 64 = 6,400 cells.

sections.heading: Immunity
sections.text: Innate immunity is the first, non-specific defence: skin, mucus, phagocytes and inflammation. Adaptive immunity is specific and has memory. B lymphocytes make antibodies, and T lymphocytes help or kill infected cells. Active immunity follows infection or vaccination and lasts. Passive immunity comes from transferred antibodies, such as maternal antibodies, and is temporary. Vaccines expose the immune system to a safe antigen, producing memory without the disease. Live, inactivated, subunit and toxoid vaccines work in different ways.

sections.heading: Vaccines and disease
sections.text: Common infectious diseases include malaria, tuberculosis, HIV and cholera. Their agents, transmission and control differ. Vaccination schedules and notifiable disease rules vary by country, so check the current national schedule and guidelines. In teaching, use safe models and clear examples, and correct myths about vaccines and antibiotics.

keyPoints: Bacteria are prokaryotes, fungi are eukaryotes, and viruses are obligate intracellular parasites.
Bacterial growth in a closed culture passes through lag, log, stationary and death phases.
Number of generations n = time ÷ generation time; final cells = starting cells × 2^n.
Sterilization kills all microbes including spores, while disinfection reduces pathogens on surfaces.
Innate immunity is non-specific and immediate; adaptive immunity is specific and has memory.
Vaccines give active immunity, and schedules vary by country, so check the national schedule.

en.title: Molecular Biology and Biotechnology
en.short: DNA, replication, gene expression, mutation, recombinant DNA, PCR, cloning, biotechnology and ethics.

sections.heading: DNA and replication
sections.text:
DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands. Each nucleotide has a sugar, phosphate and base. Bases pair A with T and G with C.

Replication is semi-conservative: each new double helix keeps one old strand and one new strand. Helicase unwinds DNA, primase makes an RNA primer, and DNA polymerase adds nucleotides 5' to 3'. The leading strand is continuous; the lagging strand forms Okazaki fragments, joined by ligase.

sections.heading: Gene expression and mutation
sections.text:
Transcription copies a gene into RNA. RNA polymerase binds a promoter and makes mRNA, processed in eukaryotes. Translation uses ribosomes and tRNA. Each codon of three bases specifies an amino acid; AUG starts and stop codons end. Gene regulation controls when and how much a gene is expressed. Bacteria use operons, such as the lac operon; eukaryotes use transcription factors and enhancers.

Mutation is a change in DNA sequence. Substitution may be silent (no change in amino acid), missense (a different amino acid) or nonsense (a stop codon). Insertion or deletion can shift the reading frame. Mutations may be inherited or caused by mutagens, and they are the source of new alleles.

sections.heading: Recombinant DNA and PCR
sections.text:
Recombinant DNA joins DNA from different sources. Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sites, DNA ligase seals the pieces, and a vector such as a plasmid carries the gene into a host cell. PCR copies a target sequence in cycles: denaturation separates strands, primers anneal, and heat-stable Taq polymerase extends them.

After n cycles, copies = starting copies × 2^n. One molecule after 10 cycles gives 1 × 2^10 = 1,024 copies; after 20 cycles, 1 × 2^20 = 1,048,576 copies. Cloning can mean making many copies of a DNA fragment, or producing a genetically identical organism.

sections.heading: Applications and ethics
sections.text:
Biotechnology uses living cells or biological molecules to make useful products or carry out useful processes. Examples include human insulin from bacteria, vaccines, diagnostic tests, improved crops, bioremediation (using microbes to clean up pollution) and forensic DNA profiling. Ethics matter: safety, consent, labelling, patenting, access and effects on small farmers. Rules differ by country, so check the national biosafety regulator.

For teaching, use models, simulations and structured debates. Ask students to separate evidence from value judgement.

keyPoints: DNA is antiparallel and pairs A with T and G with C; replication is semi-conservative.
Transcription makes RNA from a gene; translation uses codons to build a protein.
Gene regulation controls expression; mutation changes DNA sequence and may alter protein.
Recombinant DNA uses restriction enzymes, ligase and vectors to move genes between organisms.
PCR copies DNA exponentially: copies = starting copies × 2^n.
Biotechnology has real benefits and ethical limits; rules differ by country, so check the regulator.

en.title: Evolution and Systematics
en.short: Evidence for evolution, natural selection, speciation, phylogeny and systematics.

sections.heading: Evidence for evolution
sections.text:
Evolution is change in heritable characteristics of populations over generations. Evidence comes from fossils, comparative anatomy such as homologous structures, embryos, biogeography and molecular data such as DNA sequences.

Observed evolution, such as antibiotic resistance in bacteria, shows selection happening now. No single piece proves evolution alone; its strength is agreement between independent lines of evidence.

sections.heading: Natural selection
sections.text:
Natural selection is the process by which individuals with inherited traits that improve survival or reproduction in a given environment leave more offspring. It needs variation, heritability and differential reproduction. Selection acts on phenotypes but changes allele frequencies in populations.

In antibiotic resistance, bacteria with resistance genes survive treatment and multiply, so the population becomes more resistant. Selection does not create variation; mutation and recombination do.

sections.heading: Speciation
sections.text:
Speciation is the formation of new species. A species is often defined as a group whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, though this biological species concept does not fit all organisms.

Allopatric speciation follows geographic isolation, such as a river or mountain dividing a population. Sympatric speciation occurs without geographic isolation, for example by polyploidy in plants. Reproductive isolation, which stops gene flow, is the key step.

sections.heading: Systematics and trees
sections.text:
Systematics studies biological diversity and evolutionary relationships. It includes taxonomy, the naming and classification of organisms, and phylogeny, evolutionary history. Relationships are shown as phylogenetic trees or cladograms. The root is the common ancestor of all tips; each node is a common ancestor; branches lead to descendants.

A clade is an ancestor and all its descendants. Homologous traits reflect common ancestry; analogous traits, such as bat and insect wings, arise by convergent evolution. Molecular data often refine trees. In teaching, trees help correct the idea that evolution is a ladder.

keyPoints: Evolution is change in the heritable characteristics of populations over generations.
Evidence includes fossils, homologous structures, embryos, biogeography and molecular sequences.
Natural selection needs variation, heritability and differential reproduction.
Speciation requires reproductive isolation, and allopatric and sympatric are two routes.
Systematics combines taxonomy and phylogeny, and trees show common ancestry rather than a ladder.
Homologous traits reflect ancestry, while analogous traits reflect convergent evolution.

en.title: Population and Applied Genetics
en.short: Allele frequencies, quantitative traits, breeding, genetic disorders and counselling.

sections.heading: Allele frequencies
sections.text:
Population genetics studies allele and genotype frequencies in groups. For one gene with two alleles, let p and q be their frequencies, so p + q = 1. Under the Hardy-Weinberg principle, with random mating, a large population, and no mutation, migration or selection, genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q², so p² + 2pq + q² = 1. These are expectations, not laws for every real population.

Worked example: a recessive disorder affects 1 in 10,000 births, so q² = 0.0001. Then q = √0.0001 = 0.01 and p = 0.99. Carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 × 0.99 × 0.01 = 0.0198, about 2%, or roughly 1 in 50.

sections.heading: Quantitative traits and breeding
sections.text: Quantitative inheritance occurs when many genes, each with a small effect, plus the environment, shape a continuous trait such as height or crop yield. Such traits are polygenic. Heritability is the share of phenotypic variation in a given population and environment that is due to genetic variation; it is not fixed and does not describe one individual. Breeding uses selection, crossing and testing to change populations. Selective breeding keeps desirable parents. Crossbreeding may produce hybrid vigour, where offspring outperform parents, but it is not guaranteed. In class, use local crop or animal examples and simple counts.

sections.heading: Disorders and counselling
sections.text: Genetic disorders may be single-gene, chromosomal or multifactorial. Carriers of a recessive allele are usually healthy but can pass it on. Consanguinity raises the chance that both parents carry the same recessive allele. Genetic counselling is a communication process: it explains family risk, screening and options without directing the client. Counsellors protect confidentiality and refer for testing. Training and regulation vary by country, so check local rules. Ask students to read a simple pedigree and calculate one carrier risk.

keyPoints: For two alleles, p + q = 1 and Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q².
If a recessive disorder has frequency q², then q = √(q²) and carrier frequency is 2pq.
Quantitative traits are polygenic and continuous, and heritability applies to a population in a given environment.
Selective breeding and crossbreeding change populations, but hybrid vigour is not guaranteed.
Genetic counselling gives risk information and options without directing the client.
Carrier risk rises with consanguinity, and counselling rules vary by country.

en.title: Biology Curriculum and Syllabus
en.short: Curriculum models, content selection and sequencing, syllabus and scheme of work, and alignment.

sections.heading: Curriculum and aims
sections.text: A curriculum is the whole plan of learning: aims, content, teaching experiences and assessment. A syllabus is the subject document that lists aims, topics, objectives and assessment guidance. A scheme of work is the teacher’s term or weekly plan for teaching the syllabus. Curriculum models include the objectives model associated with Tyler, which starts from stated learning outcomes, and the process model associated with Stenhouse, which values inquiry and teacher judgement. Biology aims usually include knowledge, practical and inquiry skills, scientific attitudes, and application to health and environment. National aims differ, so check the official curriculum.

sections.heading: Selecting and sequencing content
sections.text: Content selection asks what biology is most worth teaching. Useful criteria include validity, significance, learnability, feasibility and balance. Sequencing arranges content so learning builds. Common principles are simple to complex, concrete to abstract, known to unknown, and spiral revisiting. For example, a teacher with a syllabus unit on ecology might plan week 1 for ecosystem components, week 2 for energy flow, week 3 for field sampling, and week 4 for a short test. Each week’s activity and assessment should match that week’s objective.

sections.heading: Reading a syllabus
sections.text: Read the syllabus as a whole before planning. Identify general aims, specific objectives, prescribed content, suggested activities, resources and assessment. Objectives should use observable verbs such as describe, explain, calculate or investigate. A scheme of work then maps units to weeks, with activities, materials and assessment. If a syllabus lists more topics than the term allows, prioritise by objectives and required practicals rather than rush coverage. Keep records and adjust after formative assessment.

sections.heading: Alignment and national differences
sections.text: Constructive alignment means objectives, teaching activities and assessment all target the same learning. If an objective says students should design an experiment, a multiple-choice test alone is not aligned. National systems differ. In Nigeria, NERDC develops school curriculum and WAEC and NECO publish examination syllabuses. Other countries have their own agencies and examination boards. Always use the current official curriculum and syllabus for your country and level.

keyPoints: A curriculum is the overall plan; a syllabus is subject-specific; a scheme of work is the teacher’s plan.
Objectives and process models are two curriculum models; biology aims include knowledge, skills, attitudes and application.
Select content by validity, significance, learnability, feasibility and balance.
Sequence from simple to complex, concrete to abstract, known to unknown, and revisit in a spiral.
Read a syllabus for aims, objectives, content, activities, resources and assessment before writing a scheme of work.
Constructive alignment matches objectives, activities and assessment; national curricula and syllabuses differ, so check current official sources.

en.title: Methods of Teaching Biology
en.short: Lesson planning, inquiry, demonstration, discussion, projects, cooperative work, questioning and practical management.

sections.heading: Planning a biology lesson
sections.text:
A lesson plan states clear learning objectives, links to prior knowledge, lists materials, and sets a timed sequence of activities with checks for understanding. Objectives should be observable: 'students will explain osmosis’ rather than 'know osmosis'. Plan grouping, room layout and safety. A plan has an introduction, development, a practical or discussion, and a closing review.

Ngozi, a trainee in Enugu, plans a lesson on transpiration. She writes two objectives, prepares a leafy shoot in a plastic bag, and times each stage.

sections.heading: Inquiry and demonstration
sections.text:
Inquiry learning starts from a question and lets students investigate, collect evidence and explain. It may be structured (teacher gives question and method), guided, or open. The 5E model (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate) is a common sequence.

Demonstration is when the teacher performs an activity while students observe and answer questions; it suits expensive, slow, rare or hazardous work. Tell students what to look for. For example, a teacher demonstrates osmosis with potato strips in salt solutions; students predict and record.

sections.heading: Discussion, projects and cooperation
sections.text:
Discussion is purposeful talk guided by the teacher, with ground rules and a clear question. The teacher facilitates, probes and summarises; it is not a free chat.

Project method gives an extended task, often producing a report or model, such as a survey of plants around the school. Cooperative learning places students in small groups with positive interdependence (each has a role) and individual accountability (each is assessed). Clear roles and a group product are essential.

sections.heading: Questioning, practicals and management
sections.text:
Questioning should include wait time (a pause after asking) and a mix of lower and higher order questions. Ask why and how to probe. Practical work gives hands-on experience; use predict, observe, explain. Before a practical, check equipment and give clear instructions.

Classroom management for science means routines for entering, distributing equipment, moving safely and clearing up. Active supervision and clear expectations prevent problems. Mr Adeyemi, teaching forty students in Ibadan, assigns group roles and uses a bell for transitions.

keyPoints: A lesson plan states observable objectives, prior knowledge, materials, timed activities and a closing review.
Inquiry starts from a question; it can be structured, guided or open, and the 5E model is one sequence.
Demonstration suits costly, slow, rare or hazardous work and needs clear focus points.
Discussion is purposeful, guided talk; projects are extended tasks with a product.
Cooperative learning needs positive interdependence and individual accountability.
Questioning uses wait time and higher-order probes; practical work uses predict, observe, explain; science lessons need routines and active supervision.

en.title: Instructional Materials and ICT in Biology
en.short: Choosing, improvising and evaluating charts, models, specimens, microscopes, videos, simulations and mobile resources.

sections.heading: Selection and purpose
sections.text: Instructional materials are resources that make learning concrete: charts, models, specimens, microscopes, videos, simulations and mobile apps. ICT means information and communication technology, such as projectors, phones, the internet and virtual laboratories. Select materials for a stated objective, not novelty. Check syllabus fit, accuracy, level, language, safety, accessibility and maintenance. Preview each resource and prepare guiding questions. A material should reduce abstraction, not add confusion.

sections.heading: Charts, models, specimens
sections.text: Charts are flat visual displays for summary, comparison and revision. Models are three-dimensional representations of structures too small, too large or unsafe to bring to class. Specimens are real biological materials, such as leaves, insects or preserved organs. They give direct experience but need safe, legal collection. Improvisation means making a resource from cheap local materials when commercial equipment is missing. For example, a teacher in Kaduna, Nigeria, might make a flower model from paper, wire and clay, checking every label against the textbook and asking a colleague to verify it. Improvised materials must be accurate, safe and durable.

sections.heading: Microscopes, video and simulations
sections.text: A microscope is an optical instrument for viewing small objects. Demonstrate parts, focusing order and safety before students practise in small groups. Videos bring motion, scale and distant places into class. Simulations are interactive computer models that let students change variables and see results. Mobile resources include apps, offline videos and messaging groups. They support revision and fieldwork, but manage data cost, screen size and distraction. ICT does not replace practical work. A virtual microscope or dissection can prepare students or substitute when equipment is scarce, but it cannot teach all manual skills. Check source and accuracy.

sections.heading: Evaluating materials
sections.text: Evaluate accuracy, cost and learning value. Accuracy means correct, current, unbiased science. Cost includes purchase, running, maintenance, consumables, training and teacher time. Learning value means clear explanation, active thinking, feedback and transfer. Use a checklist: Does it match the objective? Is it correct? Can all students use it? Is it safe? Can we afford to run and repair it?

keyPoints: Instructional materials should serve a stated learning objective and be previewed before use.
Charts, models and specimens make abstract biology concrete but must be accurate, safe and legal.
Improvisation uses cheap local materials, but an improvised resource must still be scientifically correct.
Microscopes, videos, simulations and mobile resources support learning but do not replace practical skills.
Evaluate materials for accuracy, total cost and learning value, including maintenance and teacher time.
A cheap resource that wastes lesson time or teaches wrong science has poor learning value.

en.title: Assessment and Evaluation in Biology
en.short: Formative and summative assessment, test construction, practical marking, validity and feedback.

sections.heading: Assessment and evaluation
sections.text: Assessment gathers evidence of learning. Evaluation judges quality, progress or merit from that evidence. Formative assessment happens during teaching. It is low stakes, gives feedback and helps the teacher adjust the next lesson. Summative assessment comes at the end of a unit or course and is used for grading, certification or reporting. In biology, quizzes, drawings and practical checks can be formative; terminal and practical examinations are often summative.

sections.heading: Constructing a test
sections.text:
Test construction starts from objectives. A table of specification maps topics against cognitive levels and shows the items or marks for each cell. It supports coverage and balance. Match item types to objectives: multiple-choice and short answers suit recall and understanding; essays and practical tasks suit analysis and investigation. Moderate the paper and prepare the marking scheme first.

Item analysis checks quality. With 40 students, 28 correct gives difficulty p = 28 ÷ 40 = 0.70, or 70 per cent. For the top 10 and bottom 10, 9 and 3 correct gives D = (9 − 3) ÷ 10 = 0.60. Positive D favours stronger students.

sections.heading: Practical assessment
sections.text: Practical assessment judges process and product. A checklist or analytic rubric lists criteria such as safety, apparatus handling, observation, measurement, recording, drawing, interpretation and conclusion. Prepare the marking scheme before the practical and share the criteria. For high-stakes practicals, double marking or moderation reduces marker differences. For example, a 10-mark food-test rubric might give 2 marks for safety, 3 for procedure, 3 for recording and 2 for a supported conclusion.

sections.heading: Validity, reliability and feedback
sections.text: Validity is the extent to which an assessment measures the intended learning. Content validity is supported by the table of specification. Reliability is consistency: a reliable test gives similar results on repeat occasions or with different markers. Inter-rater reliability matters in practical and essay marking. Feedback should be timely, specific and linked to criteria. Reporting should give scores with criteria and progress, not only rank. Use results to evaluate teaching and improve the course.

keyPoints: Formative assessment guides learning during teaching; summative assessment grades or certifies at the end.
A table of specification maps topics to cognitive levels and marks, improving content coverage.
Validity is whether a test measures intended learning; reliability is consistency across occasions and markers.
Item difficulty p = number correct ÷ total students; discrimination D = (upper correct − lower correct) ÷ group size.
Practical assessment should use a rubric covering process skills, recording and conclusions, with moderation for high stakes.
Feedback and reporting should be timely, specific and criterion-referenced, not only a rank order.

en.title: Laboratory Management and Fieldwork
en.short: Stocking and caring for a school biology lab, risk and waste, specimen storage, and safe fieldwork.

sections.heading: Stocking and care
sections.text: A school biology laboratory is a workplace, so organise it for safe movement and quick supervision. Keep an inventory, a written list of equipment and chemicals with amounts and locations. Set minimum stock levels and use first in, first out. Store acids and bases apart, flammables in a closed metal cabinet, and poisons locked. Label everything clearly. Care for microscopes by cleaning lenses with lens tissue, keeping them covered and dry, and checking lamps and plugs. Inspect glassware for cracks and electrical leads for damage.

sections.heading: Risk and waste
sections.text: Risk assessment means identifying hazards, deciding who may be harmed and how, and recording controls before work starts. Hazards include chemicals, heat, sharp glass, electricity, allergens and microbes. Use the lowest risk practical, provide eye protection and ventilation, and know first aid. Waste must be segregated: sharps into a sharps container, biological waste autoclaved (steam-sterilised) or incinerated, and chemical waste collected for proper disposal. Rules differ by country and school; check current local and national guidance. Never pour unknown chemicals down the sink.

sections.heading: Specimens and records
sections.text: Store specimens so they stay useful and safe. Label each with its name, date, source and preservative. Keep wet specimens sealed in preservative fluid, in a ventilated, locked store, and check levels. Dry specimens need pest-proof boxes and silica gel. Keep a loan book. A small case: a school keeps a locust collection in a sealed box with a pest deterrent, checks it each term, and records any loan. This prevents pest damage, mould and loss.

sections.heading: Safe fieldwork
sections.text: Plan fieldwork from the learning aim backwards. Visit the site first, get permission and consent, write a risk assessment, and set adult-to-student ratios under school policy. Check weather, water, terrain, toilets, transport and emergency contacts. Carry first aid and means of communication. Brief students on boundaries, clothing and behaviour. In a stream study, check depth and flow, avoid stagnant water, and do not collect protected species. Leave the site as found.

keyPoints: Keep a written inventory with minimum stock levels and use first in, first out.
Store chemicals by hazard, label everything, and lock poisons.
Clean and cover microscopes, and inspect glassware and electrical leads.
A risk assessment records hazards, who may be harmed and the controls.
Segregate sharps, biological and chemical waste and follow current local rules.
Plan fieldwork with a pre-visit, permission, risk assessment, first aid and clear boundaries.

en.title: Inclusive and Differentiated Biology Teaching
en.short: Adapting biology lessons for disability, language, gender and large classes, with fair practical work.

sections.heading: Inclusion and differentiation
sections.text: Inclusion means all learners can access, take part in and achieve in the biology curriculum. Differentiation means adjusting content, process, product or environment so each learner works at a suitable level. Scaffolding is temporary support, such as a word bank or partly completed table, removed as confidence grows. Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is a planning framework: present ideas in more than one way, allow several ways to respond, and build motivation. An individual education plan (IEP) records one learner’s goals and supports; its name and legal status vary by country.

sections.heading: Disability and language
sections.text: Adapt for the barrier, not the label. A learner with low vision needs large print, strong contrast or a tactile model. A deaf learner needs written instructions, captions and a clear line of sight. A learner with a physical disability may need adapted equipment, extra time or an assistant who supports without doing the task. For language differences, use visuals, a bilingual glossary, short sentences and pair work that lets learners explain a term in their first language before using English. Check exam language rules; they differ.

sections.heading: Gender, classes and practicals
sections.text: Use examples that show women and men equally, and avoid assuming boys prefer field work or girls prefer care work. Give all learners equal access to equipment and speaking time. In large classes, use stations, peer tutors, clear roles and local materials. Follow a whole-class demonstration with small-group tasks and rotating roles. Practical work is fair when every learner takes an active part and is assessed on what they can do. Brief safety in plain language, offer adapted tools and recording choices, and let support staff prompt rather than complete the task. Case: in a large Ibadan class, a teacher plans a germination practical. A learner with low vision gets large-print labels and a raised-line diagram; a learner still learning English gets a bilingual word list; groups rotate roles so each student observes, measures, records and reports. The teacher assesses the process.

keyPoints: Inclusion means all learners access, participate and achieve; differentiation adjusts content, process, product or environment.
UDL plans multiple ways to present ideas, allow responses and build motivation; scaffolding is temporary support.
Adapt for the specific barrier: large print or tactile models for low vision, written instructions for deaf learners, and bilingual glossaries for language differences.
In large classes use stations, peer tutors, clear rotating roles and local materials.
Fair practical work means every learner handles equipment and is assessed on process, with support staff prompting rather than doing the task.
Check your country’s law and examination rules on accommodation, because they vary.

en.title: Biology Teaching Practice: The School Practicum
en.short: Observation, lesson planning, microteaching, classroom teaching, assessment, reflection, portfolio and conduct.

sections.heading: The practicum cycle
sections.text:
Teaching practice, often called the practicum, is a supervised school placement where a trainee teacher learns by doing. The cycle usually runs through observation, planning, microteaching, classroom teaching, assessment and reflection. Observation means watching an experienced teacher with a focus, such as how questions are used, and recording evidence. Being observed means a mentor or university supervisor watches your lesson against agreed criteria. Institutions differ, so check your handbook for stages, forms and pass requirements.

A small case: Ada watches a biology teacher introduce respiration. She notes the teacher’s questions and timing. Later she plans a short peer lesson on the same topic. Her supervisor observes, gives feedback, and Ada writes what she will change. This is one turn of the cycle.

sections.heading: Planning and microteaching
sections.text: A lesson plan states objectives, prior knowledge, materials, activities, timing, assessment and differentiation. Objectives should describe what students can do, not what the teacher will cover. Microteaching is a scaled-down lesson, often taught to peers for a few minutes, then discussed. It lets you practise one skill, such as explaining a diagram or asking probing questions, before full-class teaching. Prepare safety and practical arrangements for any biology activity.

sections.heading: Classroom teaching and assessment
sections.text: In the classroom, begin with a clear opening, connect to prior learning, use varied questions, and check understanding before moving on. For practical work, give instructions and safety rules first. Assessment during teaching can be informal, such as questioning and short tasks, or formal, such as a quiz. Feedback should be specific and timely. Record results and use them to adjust the next lesson.

sections.heading: Portfolio and professional conduct
sections.text: A teaching portfolio is an organised collection of evidence: lesson plans, observation notes, feedback, assessment records, samples of learners’ work and reflections. Reflection means judging what worked, why, and what to change. Professional conduct includes punctuality, suitable dress, confidentiality, respect for learners, and following school rules and the national teacher code where one applies. Keep records honest. Do not disclose learners’ personal information.

keyPoints: Teaching practice is a supervised school placement built on a repeating cycle of observation, planning, teaching, assessment and reflection.
A lesson plan should state what learners will be able to do, with materials, timing, assessment and differentiation.
Microteaching is short peer teaching used to practise one skill before full-class lessons.
Assessment during teaching should check understanding and feed back into the next lesson.
A portfolio collects honest evidence such as plans, observation notes, feedback and reflections.
Professional conduct includes punctuality, confidentiality, respect and following school rules and the applicable teacher code.

en.title: Research Methods in Biology Education
en.short: Designs, sampling, instruments, data collection, ethics and simple analysis for small biology education studies.

sections.heading: Planning a study
sections.text: Begin with a clear research question: Does guided practical work improve Year 10 students’ understanding of osmosis? Read existing work, then choose a design. A descriptive design records what exists. A correlational design tests whether two measured variables move together. An experimental design compares a treatment with a control. A quasi-experimental design uses existing classes because random assignment is often impossible in schools. Action research is a teacher’s plan, act, observe and reflect cycle to improve practice.

sections.heading: Sampling and instruments
sections.text: The population is everyone you want to describe; the sample is the smaller group you study. Random sampling gives every member a known chance of selection. Stratified sampling divides the population into groups, such as year levels, then samples within each. Convenience sampling uses whoever is available; it is common but weak for generalisation. Instruments include questionnaires, interviews, observation checklists and tests. Validity means measuring what is claimed; reliability means giving consistent results. Pilot the instrument and revise unclear items.

sections.heading: Collecting and analysing
sections.text: Collect data under the same conditions for all participants. Keep records, code responses and check for missing values. For quantitative data, report descriptive statistics. The mean is the sum of scores divided by the number of scores. A percentage is part ÷ whole × 100. If 24 of 40 students pass a practical test, the pass rate is 24 ÷ 40 × 100 = 60%. For qualitative data, group similar responses into themes and quote examples. Do not claim cause from correlation alone.

sections.heading: Ethics and reporting
sections.text: Seek informed consent, explain the purpose and allow withdrawal. Protect anonymity and confidentiality. For participants under 18, obtain parental or guardian consent and the school’s permission. Avoid harm and deception. Get approval from your institution’s ethics committee where required. Report methods, results and limitations honestly. A small study cannot prove a general law, so state what your sample and design allow you to conclude.

keyPoints: A research question should name the group, the issue or intervention, and what you will measure.
Random sampling gives every member a known chance; convenience sampling limits generalisation.
Validity means measuring what is claimed; reliability means consistency.
Mean = sum of scores ÷ number of scores; percentage = part ÷ whole × 100.
Informed consent, confidentiality and ethics approval protect participants.
Correlation alone does not show cause; report limitations honestly.

en.title: Ethics and Professionalism in Biology Education
en.short: Professional codes, academic integrity, safety and consent, fair teaching, and sensitive biology topics.

sections.heading: Professional codes
sections.text: A professional code is a written set of standards and duties for teachers. It usually covers honesty, competence, care, confidentiality and respect. In Nigeria the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) regulates teachers and has a code of conduct; other countries have their own bodies. Read the current code for your country and school. A code guides judgement but does not replace the law or child-protection policy.

sections.heading: Academic integrity
sections.text: Academic integrity means honest work in study, teaching and research. Students must not plagiarise, which is presenting another person’s words or ideas as their own, and must not fabricate or falsify data. In practicals, record results as they are, keep raw data and cite sources. Teachers should model this and apply published rules consistently. Case: Amina copies a genetics report. The fair response is to teach citation and apply the policy, not to shame her publicly.

sections.heading: Safety and consent
sections.text: Practical work needs a risk assessment, a check of hazards and controls before the lesson.
